subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: If water flows in at a known rate for six hours, how much water arrived? Multiply rate by time — unless the rate keeps changing. The definite integral is what 'rate times time' becomes when the rate refuses to hold still, and it is the second pillar of calculus.
learning_objectives: Interpret the definite integral as accumulated change from a rate function
Read definite integrals as signed areas between a curve and the x-axis
Evaluate integrals geometrically using areas of triangles, rectangles, and circles
Apply integral properties: linearity, interval splitting, and reversed bounds
Translate between accumulation language and integral notation in both directions

sections.title: Accumulating a Changing Rate
sections.subtitle: From rate × time to the integral
sections.body:
A constant inflow of 5 L/min for 6 minutes delivers 30 liters: rate times time, the area of a 5-by-6 rectangle on the rate graph. When the rate R(t) varies, no single multiplication works — but slicing time into tiny intervals, multiplying each slice's (nearly constant) rate by its duration, and adding recovers the idea: total ≈ Σ R(tᵢ)Δt. As slices shrink, the sum sharpens into the definite integral ∫₀⁶ R(t) dt — the exact accumulated change.

The notation narrates the construction: the integral sign ∫ is an elongated S for 'sum,' R(t) dt echoes rate-times-tiny-duration, and the bounds 0 and 6 mark the accumulation window. Reading ∫ₐᵇ R(t) dt aloud as 'the total change accumulated from a to b' is the habit that keeps every applied problem honest.

The units multiply accordingly: liters per minute times minutes gives liters — integral units are ALWAYS (integrand units) × (variable units). A rate in cars per hour integrated over hours counts cars; force in newtons integrated over meters yields newton-meters (work). The units check is the fastest sanity test on any applied integral.

The AP's central translation pair, run in both directions: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt ('final equals initial plus accumulated change') and ∫ₐᵇ f'(t) dt = f(b) - f(a) ('the integral of a rate is the net change'). These sentences anchor Unit 8's applications and appear on virtually every modern FRQ set; learn them as English, not just symbols.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f(t) dt: the limit of rate-times-duration sums — exact accumulated change
Integral units = integrand units × variable units (L/min × min = L)
f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' dt and its rearrangement — the applied workhorse
boxes: ap_alert

'How much water is in the tank at t = 6?' is f(0) + ∫₀⁶ R(t) dt — initial PLUS accumulation. Forgetting the initial amount is the most common applied-integral error on the exam; the phrase 'plus what was already there' belongs in your setup line.

sections.title: Signed Area
sections.subtitle: What the integral measures on a graph
sections.body:
Geometrically, ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx is the SIGNED area between the curve and the x-axis: regions above the axis count positive, regions below count negative. A rate dipping below zero (water draining, particle moving left) subtracts from the accumulation, and the graph shows the subtraction as below-axis area.

Signed versus total area is the unit's recurring distinction. ∫₀⁴ f dx with f positive on (0, 1) and negative on (1, 4) nets the difference; the TOTAL area enclosed requires ∫|f| — splitting at the zero crossing and flipping the negative piece's sign. The motion translation: integral of velocity is displacement (signed); integral of speed |v| is total distance — Unit 4's distinction, now in integral form.

Geometric evaluation handles the AP's favorite integral format: a piecewise-linear or circular graph of f, with integrals computed from area formulas. Triangles (½bh), rectangles, trapezoids, and — the perennial — semicircles and quarter circles (areas ¼πr², ½πr² read off the figure). Below-axis pieces enter negative: a quarter circle of radius 2 below the axis contributes -π.

The graph-reading protocol: mark the zero crossings, name each region's shape, compute each area, attach signs, add. Five steps, no antiderivatives — and the format appears on every exam because it tests the integral's MEANING rather than its mechanics.
key_terms: Above-axis positive, below-axis negative — the integral's geometric content
Total area integrates |f|: split at zeros, flip negative pieces
Triangles, trapezoids, circle parts — areas read from the figure, signs attached
boxes: ap_alert

Circle pieces in graph-integrals are radius-traps: a semicircular arc spanning [2, 6] has radius 2 (half the span), not 4. Mark the radius on the figure before computing ¼πr² or ½πr² — the misread radius quadruples the area and the error.

sections.title: The Rules of Accumulation
sections.subtitle: Properties that move integrals around
sections.body:
Linearity: ∫(f + g) = ∫f + ∫g and ∫cf = c∫f — integrals split over sums and release constants, exactly like derivatives and for the same limit-law reasons. Splitting: ∫ₐᵇ + ∫ᵦᶜ = ∫ₐᶜ — accumulation over adjacent windows adds, even when b sits OUTSIDE [a, c] (the algebra self-corrects via signs). Reversal: ∫ᵇₐ = -∫ₐᵇ — swapping bounds flips the sign, because accumulating backward undoes.

Two degenerate facts complete the kit: ∫ₐᵃ f = 0 (no window, no accumulation) and the comparison property — if f ≤ g on [a, b], then ∫ₐᵇ f ≤ ∫ₐᵇ g. It powers quick bounds: since 1 ≤ √(1 + x³) ≤ 1 + x³ on [0, 1], the integral of the middle expression is trapped between 1 and 7/4. Bounding integrands bounds integrals — a BC habit that returns in error analysis.

The properties' exam format is the given-values puzzle: knowing ∫₀⁵ f = 12 and ∫₃⁵ f = 4, find ∫₀³ f (answer: 8, by splitting) or ∫₅⁰ 2f (answer: -24, by reversal and linearity). No functions appear — only the algebra of accumulation. Treat the integrals as numbers with bookkeeping rules and the puzzles are arithmetic.

One caution mirrors the derivative side: integrals do NOT split over products or quotients — ∫fg ≠ (∫f)(∫g). The product's integral machinery (integration by parts) waits in chapter 6; until then, products inside integrals are a stop sign, not an invitation to improvise.
key_terms: Splits over sums, releases constant factors — like differentiation
Adjacent windows add; swapped bounds negate
boxes: ap_alert

Given-values puzzles hide the reversal trick: ∫₇² f dx is the negative of the given ∫₂⁷ f dx. Scan the bounds' ORDER before any arithmetic — the flipped-bounds sign error is silent and costs the whole point.

sections.title: The Accumulation Function
sections.subtitle: Integrals with a variable top
sections.body:
Fix the lower bound and let the upper bound roam: g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt defines a FUNCTION of x — the accumulation function, measuring how much f-area has piled up from a to x. As x sweeps right, g grows where f is positive (area accruing), falls where f is negative, and pauses where f is zero. The variable t inside is a dummy; x lives only in the bound.

Reading g from a graph of f is a tested skill in its own right: g's value at x is the signed area so far — so g has a maximum where f crosses from + to − (accumulation peaks when the deposits turn to withdrawals), g is increasing where f > 0, and g inflects where f has an extreme. The translation table from Unit 5's graph-of-f' genre applies VERBATIM with f playing the role of g's derivative — which the next chapter's Fundamental Theorem will make official.

Worked reading: f piecewise-linear, positive triangle of area 6 on [0, 3], negative triangle of area 2 on [3, 5]. Then g(0) = 0, g(3) = 6 (the peak), g(5) = 4 — climbing to 6, easing back to 4. Asked for g's maximum on [0, 5]: x = 3, 'because g' = f changes from positive to negative there' — Unit 5's justification grammar, one derivative down.

The accumulation function is the unit's conceptual hinge: it converts integrals from numbers into functions, sets up FTC Part 1 (what is g'?), and models real quantities — total rainfall by day x, cars passed by time x — that FRQs describe in exactly this form. The format rewards students who see 'integral with x on top' and immediately think 'a function whose derivative is the integrand.'
key_terms: g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt: area-so-far as a function of the sweeping bound
The t inside is internal bookkeeping; the function's variable is the bound x
f acts as g's derivative: f's signs/crossings dictate g's rises/extremes
boxes: ap_alert

For g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt with f given graphically, every Unit 5 question reappears: g increasing where f > 0, g's max where f crosses downward, g's inflections at f's extremes. One memorized correspondence, an entire FRQ genre unlocked.

mcq.question: Water enters a tank at R(t) = 4 + 2t L/min. The amount added between t = 0 and t = 3 is
mcq.explanation: ∫₀³ (4 + 2t) dt — geometrically a trapezoid with parallel sides 4 and 10 over width 3: ½(4 + 10)(3) = 21.

mcq.question: The graph of f consists of a triangle of area 8 above the axis on [0, 4] and a triangle of area 3 below the axis on [4, 6]. ∫₀⁶ f(x) dx =
mcq.explanation: Signed area: +8 - 3 = 5. (Total area would be 11 — the |f| version.)

mcq.question: Given ∫₁⁸ f dx = 10 and ∫₁⁵ f dx = 7, then ∫₈⁵ f dx =
mcq.explanation: ∫₅⁸ f = 10 - 7 = 3 by splitting; reversing the bounds negates: -3.

mcq.question: g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt where f is positive on (0, 2), negative on (2, 7). The maximum of g on [0, 7] occurs at x =
mcq.explanation: g climbs while f > 0 and falls after: the accumulation peaks at the downward crossing x = 2.

mcq.question: The graph of f on [0, 4] is the upper semicircle of radius 2 centered at (2, 0). ∫₀⁴ f(x) dx =
mcq.explanation: Half a circle of radius 2: ½π(2²) = 2π, all above the axis.

frq.question:
The rate at which customers enter a store is modeled by a piecewise-linear function E(t) (customers per hour): E rises linearly from E(0) = 0 to E(2) = 60, stays at 60 until t = 5, then falls linearly to E(8) = 0.
(a) Compute ∫₀⁸ E(t) dt using geometry, and interpret the result with units.
(b) The store opened with 12 customers inside, and customers leave at a constant 40 per hour for the whole period. Write an expression for the number of customers inside at time t = 8 and evaluate it.
(c) At what time t is the number of customers inside greatest? Justify with rates.
rubric: (a) Trapezoid: ½(8 + 3)(60) = 330 customers entered
(c) Inside-count rate is E(t) - 40; greatest when the rate changes + to −
E(t) = 40 falling: t = 6 (on the descent from 60 at t=5 to 0 at t=8, E hits 40 at t = 6); justified as sign change of E - 40
frq.model_answer: (a) The region under E is a trapezoid with parallel sides of lengths 8 (the full base, 0 to 8) and 3 (the top, 2 to 5) and height 60: ∫₀⁸ E dt = ½(8 + 3)(60) = 330. In context: 330 customers entered the store during the 8 hours. (b) Inside at t = 8: initial + entered − left = 12 + 330 - 40(8) = 12 + 330 - 320 = 22 customers. (c) The count inside changes at rate E(t) - 40. E - 40 > 0 once E exceeds 40 (at t = 4/3 on the rise) and stays positive until E falls back to 40: on the descent E(t) = 60 - 20(t - 5), which equals 40 at t = 6. The rate flips from + to − at t = 6, so the store is fullest at t = 6 hours.

frq.question:
The graph of f on [-4, 4] consists of three pieces: a semicircle of radius 1 centered at (-3, 0) lying below the x-axis from (-4, 0) to (-2, 0); a line segment from (-2, 0) to (0, 2); and a line segment from (0, 2) to (4, -2).
(a) Evaluate ∫₋₄⁻² f, ∫₋₂⁰ f, and ∫₀⁴ f.
(b) Evaluate ∫₋₄⁴ f(x) dx.
(c) Find the total area between f and the x-axis on [-4, 4].
rubric: (a) Semicircle below: -π/2; triangle: +2; the [0,4] piece crosses zero at x = 2: +2 then -2, net 0
(c) Total area: π/2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 + π/2
Zero crossing at x = 2 identified and used to split
frq.model_answer: (a) The semicircle of radius 1 below the axis contributes -½π(1²) = -π/2. The triangle from (-2, 0) to (0, 2) has area ½(2)(2) = 2, above the axis: +2. On [0, 4], the line from (0, 2) to (4, -2) crosses zero at x = 2: a positive triangle ½(2)(2) = +2 then a negative one -2: net 0. (b) ∫₋₄⁴ f = -π/2 + 2 + 0 = 2 - π/2. (c) Total (unsigned) area: π/2 + 2 + 2 + 2 = 6 + π/2.

frq.question:
Let g(x) = ∫₂ˣ f(t) dt, where f is graphed: f is positive on (0, 3), zero at 3, negative on (3, 7), with ∫₂³ f = 5 and ∫₃⁷ f = -9.
(a) Compute g(2), g(3), and g(7).
(b) On what interval is g increasing? Justify in terms of f.
(c) Find the minimum value of g on [2, 7], with justification.
rubric: (b) g increasing where f > 0: on (2, 3)
(c) Candidates: endpoints and the sign change; g falls from 5 throughout (3,7)
Minimum g(7) = -4, since g decreases on (3, 7) and ends lowest there
frq.model_answer: (a) g(2) = ∫₂² f = 0. g(3) = ∫₂³ f = 5. g(7) = ∫₂⁷ f = 5 + (-9) = -4. (b) g grows exactly where new area is positive — where f > 0: the interval (2, 3). (c) g rises to 5 at x = 3, then falls steadily across (3, 7) (f < 0 there) to g(7) = -4. The candidates for the minimum are x = 2 (value 0) and x = 7 (value -4): the minimum value is -4 at x = 7, justified because g' = f < 0 on (3, 7) makes g strictly decreasing after its peak, so the right endpoint is lowest.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Before integrals had antiderivatives, they had rectangles. Riemann sums approximate area with arithmetic anyone can do — and the AP grades the setup, the over/under reasoning, and the trapezoid upgrade every single year.
learning_objectives: Construct left, right, and midpoint Riemann sums from formulas and tables
Compute trapezoidal approximations, including unequal subinterval widths
Determine over/underestimate direction from monotonicity (rectangles) and concavity (trapezoids)
Express a definite integral as a limit of Riemann sums and vice versa
Choose sample points and widths correctly from table data on the exam's terms

sections.title: Rectangles Under a Curve
sections.subtitle: Left, right, and midpoint sums
sections.body:
Slice [a, b] into n subintervals of width Δx = (b - a)/n and erect a rectangle on each, with height read from f at a chosen sample point: the LEFT endpoint (left Riemann sum), RIGHT endpoint (right sum), or MIDPOINT (midpoint sum). Each rectangle contributes height × width; the sum approximates ∫ₐᵇ f dx, with the choice of sample point setting the bias.

Worked on f(x) = x² over [0, 2] with n = 4 (Δx = ½): left sum uses heights at 0, ½, 1, 3/2: (0 + ¼ + 1 + 9/4)(½) = 7/4 = 1.75. Right sum uses ½, 1, 3/2, 2: (¼ + 1 + 9/4 + 4)(½) = 15/4 = 3.75. The true value (next chapters) is 8/3 ≈ 2.67 — bracketed by the two, as an increasing function guarantees. Midpoint, using ¼, ¾, 5/4, 7/4: (1/16 + 9/16 + 25/16 + 49/16)(½) = 84/32 = 2.625 — strikingly closer, a pattern that is no accident.

From tables — the AP's preferred delivery — the subintervals come pre-cut by the data, often with UNEQUAL widths: t-values 0, 2, 5, 6 give widths 2, 3, 1, and each rectangle's width must be read individually. The left sum uses each subinterval's left-edge value; no Δx formula applies. Unequal widths are the norm on FRQs, and hard-coding (b-a)/n is the trap.

Indexing discipline prevents the classic off-by-one: with n subintervals, a left sum uses values at the first n points (skipping the last), a right sum the last n (skipping the first). Writing the sample values in a row and bracketing which n get used beats any formula memorized blind.
key_terms: Σ f(sample)·width over the subintervals — rectangle areas standing in for the integral
Left, right, or midpoint of each subinterval sets the rectangle heights and the bias
Table data pre-cuts the intervals; each width is read, not computed from (b-a)/n
boxes: ap_alert

Table-based Riemann FRQs grade the SETUP: write the sum as height₁·width₁ + height₂·width₂ + ⋯ with the actual numbers visible. A bare final answer cannot earn the setup point, and with unequal widths the visible setup is also your own error-catcher.

sections.title: Over or Under, Part 1
sections.subtitle: Monotonicity decides for rectangles
sections.body:
For an INCREASING function, every left-endpoint rectangle sits below the curve (the left edge is the interval's lowest point): the left sum UNDERestimates, and symmetrically the right sum OVERestimates. For a DECREASING function, the roles flip: left over, right under. The mnemonic is unnecessary if you sketch one subinterval — but the conclusion sentence is graded, so the reasoning must be stated, not just used.

The graded sentence pattern: 'Since f is increasing on [a, b], the left Riemann sum underestimates ∫ₐᵇ f dx.' Cause (monotonicity), claim (direction). On table problems, monotonicity is read from the data (values steadily rising); on formula problems, from f' > 0. Either certificate works; one must appear.

Non-monotonic intervals void the simple rules: a function rising then falling can make a left sum land on either side. Exam questions either keep f monotone or split the analysis at the turn — and 'no conclusion without monotonicity' is itself a tested answer choice. The honest reflex: check the behavior FIRST, then claim a direction.

Midpoint sums resist monotonicity analysis (the midpoint rectangle overshoots on one half, undershoots on the other) — their bias is governed by CONCAVITY: for concave-up f, midpoint underestimates; concave-down, overestimates. The full midpoint story pairs with trapezoids in the next section, where the two make opposite errors and the geometry explains both at once.
key_terms: Left edges are minima of rising intervals; right edges are maxima
The direction claim must cite monotonicity (or the data trend) explicitly
No simple over/under verdict on intervals where f turns around
boxes: ap_alert

The over/under sentence is its own rubric point and must include the word 'increasing' or 'decreasing' (or the data-trend equivalent). 'Left sums underestimate' as a bare slogan is FALSE for decreasing functions — and the exam rotates both cases deliberately.

sections.title: Trapezoids and the Midpoint Duel
sections.subtitle: Slanted tops, concavity bias
sections.body:
Replace each rectangle's flat top with a slanted segment joining the curve's values at both edges: the trapezoid sum, T = Σ ½(f(left) + f(right))·width. Equivalently, T is the average of the left and right sums when widths are equal. Trapezoids hug curves far better than rectangles — error shrinks like 1/n² versus 1/n — and the AP uses them as the default 'good' approximation on table problems.

Trapezoid bias is pure concavity: on a CONCAVE-DOWN arc, the chord joining two curve points sags below the arc, so the trapezoid UNDERestimates; concave-up, chords sit above arcs — overestimate. (Chords below arcs for caps, above for cups: the tangent-line picture from linearization, mirrored — tangents and chords always bracket the curve from opposite sides.)

The midpoint sum makes exactly the OPPOSITE error: the midpoint rectangle equals (in area) the tangent-line trapezoid at the midpoint, and tangents sit below cups, above caps. So for concave-up f: midpoint under, trapezoid over — and the true integral lies between them, with the midpoint typically about half as wrong. The bracket-by-opposites structure is a BC-flavored insight the exam rewards in 'which is largest?' rankings.

The ranking question, assembled: for f increasing and concave up on [a, b], order L < M < ∫ < T < R. Left/right from monotonicity, mid/trap from concavity. Any specific case can be re-derived in seconds from the two principles — derive, don't memorize, because the exam permutes the function's behavior precisely to break memorized orderings.
key_terms: Σ ½(f(L) + f(R))·width — chord-topped slices, the average of L and R sums
Chords under caps (trap under), over cups (trap over); midpoint mirrors it
Midpoint and trapezoid err oppositely; the integral sits between
boxes: ap_alert

Trapezoid questions on tables with UNEQUAL widths must be computed trapezoid-by-trapezoid: ½(f₀ + f₁)w₁ + ½(f₁ + f₂)w₂ + ⋯. The averaged-sums shortcut T = (L + R)/2 silently assumes equal widths — using it on FRQ tables is a wrong answer, not a shortcut.

sections.title: The Limit Definition
sections.subtitle: Sums become integrals, and back
sections.body:
The definite integral IS the limit: ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = lim n→∞ Σᵢ f(xᵢ*)Δx — rectangles refined until the approximation error vanishes. The definition matters operationally on the AP in one specific genre: converting between limit-of-sum notation and integral notation, in both directions.

Reading a limit as an integral: lim n→∞ Σ (3/n)·√(1 + 3i/n) — the factor 3/n is Δx, so the interval has length 3; the sample 1 + 3i/n starts at 1 (right endpoints), so [a, b] = [1, 4] and the integrand is √x: the limit equals ∫₁⁴ √x dx. The decode recipe: identify Δx for the length, the sample expression's range for the bounds, and the function applied to the sample for the integrand.

Writing an integral as a limit reverses the recipe: ∫₂⁵ x³ dx = lim Σ (3/n)(2 + 3i/n)³ with right endpoints. The skeleton — Δx = (b-a)/n, xᵢ = a + iΔx, sum f(xᵢ)Δx — assembles any such expression. Both directions appear as multiple choice; the decode direction is the more common and the more fumbled.

Why the definition earns its keep beyond notation: it is what makes the integral MEAN accumulated change (chapter 1's slicing argument, formalized), it justifies every numerical method in this chapter, and it returns in BC's arc length and surface integrals where slicing arguments construct new integral formulas from scratch. The rectangles never really leave; they just go backstage.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f dx = lim Σ f(xᵢ*)Δx — the integral as refined rectangle sums
Δx gives the length; the sample's range gives the bounds; the applied function is the integrand
The definition's pattern builds new integral formulas (arc length, volumes) later
boxes: ap_alert

In limit-to-integral decodes, the bounds hide in the SAMPLE expression: 2 + 3i/n runs from 2 to 5 as i runs 1 to n — bounds [2, 5], length 3, matching Δx = 3/n. Cross-check length against Δx every time; mismatches expose a misread.

mcq.question: Using the table t: 0, 2, 5, 6 with f(t): 3, 7, 11, 9, the left Riemann sum for ∫₀⁶ f dt is
f is decreasing on [1, 9]. The right Riemann sum for ∫₁⁹ f dx is
mcq.explanation: For decreasing f, each right edge is the interval's lowest point: rectangles sit below the curve.

mcq.question: f is concave down on [0, 8]. The trapezoidal approximation of ∫₀⁸ f dx is
mcq.explanation: Chords sag below concave-down arcs: trapezoid tops sit under the curve. (Monotonicity is irrelevant for trapezoids.)

mcq.question: Using the same table as before (t: 0, 2, 5, 6; f: 3, 7, 11, 9), the trapezoidal approximation of ∫₀⁶ f dt is
lim n→∞ Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (2/n)·(1 + 2i/n)² equals
mcq.explanation: Δx = 2/n (length 2); samples 1 + 2i/n sweep (1, 3]: bounds [1, 3]; the function applied is squaring. (D is also equivalent by substitution but A is the direct decode; on the exam only one appears.)

frq.question:
A pump's flow rate R(t) (gallons per minute) is recorded: t = 0, 3, 4, 7, 10 with R = 20, 26, 28, 22, 16.
(a) Approximate ∫₀¹⁰ R(t) dt with a right Riemann sum using the four subintervals given, and interpret the result.
(b) Approximate the same integral with a trapezoidal sum.
(c) The pump's rate is known to have been increasing on [0, 4] and decreasing on [4, 10]. Can you determine whether your answer to (a) over- or underestimates on the FULL interval? Analyze each piece.
rubric: (c) On [0,4] (increasing): right sum over; on [4,10] (decreasing): right sum under
Conclusion: opposing biases — no overall verdict without more information
frq.model_answer: (a) Right sum with widths 3, 1, 3, 3 and right heights 26, 28, 22, 16: 26(3) + 28(1) + 22(3) + 16(3) = 220. Approximately 220 gallons flowed through the pump during the 10 minutes. (b) Trapezoids: ½(20+26)(3) + ½(26+28)(1) + ½(28+22)(3) + ½(22+16)(3) = 69 + 27 + 75 + 57 = 228 gallons. (c) On [0, 4], R increases, so right rectangles OVERestimate that portion; on [4, 10], R decreases, so right rectangles UNDERestimate there. The two biases oppose, and without knowing the relative sizes of the errors, no over/under verdict applies to the full-interval estimate — the honest answer is that the direction cannot be determined.

frq.question:
Let f(x) = e^{-x²} on [0, 2], a positive, decreasing, initially concave-down function with an inflection at x = 1/√2.
(a) With n = 4 equal subintervals, write (do not evaluate) the left Riemann sum for ∫₀² f dx.
(b) State whether the left sum over- or underestimates the integral, with justification.
(c) Rank L (left), T (trapezoid), and the true integral I on [0, 1/√2] only — where f is concave down — from smallest to largest, justifying each comparison.
rubric: (b) f decreasing ⟹ left endpoints are maxima ⟹ overestimate
(c) On concave-down: T < I (chords sag); f decreasing: L > I
Ranking: T < I < L
frq.model_answer: (a) Δx = ½: L = ½[e⁰ + e^{-1/4} + e^{-1} + e^{-9/4}]. (b) f is decreasing on [0, 2], so each left endpoint gives the subinterval's largest value — the rectangles poke above the curve: the left sum OVERestimates. (c) On [0, 1/√2], f is concave down: trapezoid chords sag below the arc, so T < I. f is decreasing there, so the left sum overshoots: L > I. Ranking: T < I < L.

frq.question:
Consider lim n→∞ Σᵢ₌₁ⁿ (5/n)·sin(π(2 + 5i/n)).
(a) Identify Δx, the interval [a, b], and the integrand, and rewrite the limit as a definite integral.
(b) A student claims the interval is [0, 5] 'because the sum runs from i = 1 to n.' Explain the error.
(c) Without evaluating, state whether the integral is positive, negative, or requires more analysis, given that sin is being sampled over the resulting interval.
rubric: (a) Δx = 5/n; samples 2 + 5i/n sweep (2, 7]: ∫₂⁷ sin(πx) dx
(b) The index range sets the COUNT of rectangles; the BOUNDS come from the sample expression's sweep, 2 to 7
(c) sin(πx) completes full periods on intervals of length 2; [2, 7] is 2.5 periods
Full periods cancel; the leftover [6, 7] gives ∫ sin(πx) > 0 on (6,7)? sin(πx) on (6,7): πx in (6π,7π), sine positive there — integral positive
frq.model_answer: (a) Δx = 5/n, so the interval has length 5; the sample 2 + 5i/n runs from just above 2 (i = 1) to 7 (i = n): [a, b] = [2, 7], right endpoints. The function applied is sin(π·). The limit equals ∫₂⁷ sin(πx) dx. (b) The summation index i counts the n rectangles — it never names the x-interval. The bounds live inside the sample expression: as i sweeps 1 to n, the sample sweeps 2 to 7. Reading bounds from the index is the standard decode error. (c) sin(πx) has period 2, and [2, 7] spans 2.5 periods. Each complete period integrates to zero, leaving ∫₆⁷ sin(πx) dx; on (6, 7), πx lies in (6π, 7π) where sine is positive. The integral is positive (its value is 2/π, though no evaluation was required).

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Part 1
hook: Here is the theorem that earns the adjective: the derivative of an accumulation function is the function being accumulated. Slopes and areas — built from opposite ends of calculus — turn out to be inverse operations, and everything after this page depends on it.
learning_objectives: State FTC Part 1: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x) for continuous f
Differentiate accumulation functions, including chain-rule upper bounds
Handle variable lower bounds and two-variable-bound integrals
Analyze accumulation functions (extremes, concavity) using FTC-supplied derivatives
Explain the theorem's meaning: accumulation rate equals the current integrand value

sections.title: The Theorem and Its Meaning
sections.subtitle: Why accumulation differentiates to the integrand
sections.body:
FTC Part 1: if f is continuous on an interval containing a, then g(x) = ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt is differentiable and g'(x) = f(x). Differentiating an accumulation function hands back the integrand, evaluated at the sweeping bound. Integration and differentiation are inverse processes — the fact that makes antiderivatives compute areas (Part 2, next chapter) and makes the last chapter's graph-reading correspondences exact.

The intuition deserves to be owned, not memorized: g(x + h) - g(x) is the area of the sliver between x and x + h — a near-rectangle of height f(x) and width h. So the difference quotient (g(x+h) - g(x))/h ≈ f(x)·h/h = f(x), and the limit seals it. The accumulation's growth RATE is the current deposit rate: if water pours at 7 L/min right now, the total's rate of change is 7 L/min right now. Stated that way, the deepest theorem in the course sounds obvious — which is exactly the right way to remember it.

The dummy-variable hygiene from chapter 1 pays off here: in d/dx ∫₂ˣ cos(t²) dt = cos(x²), the t was internal; the answer substitutes the BOUND into the integrand. No antiderivative of cos(t²) exists in elementary terms — and none is needed. FTC1 differentiates integrals you could never evaluate, which is precisely its working power on the exam.

Immediate dividends: every chapter-1 graph correspondence ('g has a max where f crosses + to −') is now literally Unit 5's first-derivative test applied to g' = f. The machinery was never an analogy; it was the theorem, previewed.
key_terms: d/dx ∫ₐˣ f(t) dt = f(x): the accumulation's derivative is the integrand at the bound
g(x+h) - g(x) ≈ f(x)·h: the next sliver of area is a thin rectangle
FTC1 differentiates ∫ cos(t²) dt and friends — no antiderivative required
boxes: ap_alert

d/dx ∫₅ˣ √(1 + t³) dt = √(1 + x³). One substitution, done. Students who try to FIND an antiderivative first are answering a much harder question than was asked — FTC1 problems are recognition problems, not integration problems.

sections.title: Chain Rule Upper Bounds
sections.subtitle: When x² rides on top
sections.body:
When the upper bound is a FUNCTION of x, the accumulation is a composition and the chain rule collects its fee: d/dx ∫ₐ^{u(x)} f(t) dt = f(u(x))·u'(x). Substitute the bound into the integrand, multiply by the bound's derivative. For F(x) = ∫₀^{x²} sin(t) dt: F'(x) = sin(x²)·2x.

The structure is g(u(x)) with g the plain accumulation function: FTC1 gives g' = f, the chain rule glues on u'. Seeing the two-layer anatomy keeps the formula from being one more memorized incantation — it is Unit 3's chain rule meeting this chapter's theorem, nothing new under the hood.

Variable LOWER bounds flip sign first: ∫_{v(x)}^{b} f dt = -∫_b^{v(x)} f dt, so its derivative is -f(v(x))·v'(x). Both bounds variable splits at any convenient constant: d/dx ∫_{v(x)}^{u(x)} f dt = f(u(x))·u'(x) - f(v(x))·v'(x) — 'top in, times top-prime, MINUS bottom in, times bottom-prime.' The two-bound formula compresses the whole section.

Worked at full strength: d/dx ∫_{√x}^{x³} ln(1 + t²) dt = ln(1 + x⁶)·3x² - ln(1 + x)·(1/(2√x)). Mechanical once the anatomy is seen: each bound contributes (integrand at bound)·(bound's derivative), signed by its position. Exam variants stop at one variable bound plus a constant — the full two-bound version is BC-comfortable insurance.
key_terms: d/dx ∫ₐ^{u} f dt = f(u)·u' — substitute the bound, pay its fee
Variable bottoms differentiate with a minus: -f(v)·v'
Top-in times top-prime, minus bottom-in times bottom-prime
boxes: ap_alert

The chain-rule fee on FTC1 problems is the unit's most-planted distractor: d/dx ∫₀^{x²} sin t dt = sin(x²)·2x, and the fee-free sin(x²) sits among the choices every time. Bound a function of x? Fee due. No exceptions.

sections.title: Analyzing Accumulation Functions
sections.subtitle: Unit 5's machinery, fully powered
sections.body:
With g' = f in hand officially, every analytical question about g routes through f. Critical points of g: zeros and sign changes of f. g increasing: f > 0. Concavity of g: monotonicity of f (g'' = f'). Inflections of g: extremes of f. The complete Unit 5 playbook applies with the graph of f as the given — and this composite IS the AP's single most reliable FRQ, appearing in some form nearly every year.

The standard problem hands you a piecewise graph of f (lines and circle arcs) and g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt, then walks the ladder: evaluate g at named points (geometric areas with signs), find where g is increasing (f > 0), classify g's critical points (f's crossings, by the 1DT), locate g's inflections (f's extremes), and sketch or bound g. Each rung is a chapter already taught; the FRQ is an assembly test.

Justification grammar carries over verbatim with g' = f cited: 'g has a local maximum at x = 3 because g'(x) = f(x) changes from positive to negative at x = 3.' The phrase g' = f — the theorem's invocation — is part of the graded sentence. Concavity answers cite f's behavior: 'g is concave down on (1, 4) because g' = f is decreasing there.'

Extreme-value versions add the candidates test: absolute extremes of g on [0, 8] compare g's values at endpoints and at f's sign changes, with g-values computed as accumulated areas. The arithmetic is chapter 1; the candidate logic is Unit 5; the bridge is the theorem. Three units in one problem — the reason this FRQ genre decides scores.
key_terms: Evaluate g, analyze g's behavior, classify, sketch — all from f's graph
'g'(x) = f(x)' appears in every justification — the theorem is cited, not assumed
Absolute extremes of g: compare accumulated-area values at crossings and endpoints
boxes: ap_alert

On accumulation FRQs, write 'g'(x) = f(x) by the Fundamental Theorem' once at the top of your work, then reference it. The single line activates Unit 5 grammar for every subsequent part and collects the theorem-citation point examiners look for.

sections.title: Defined by Integrals
sections.subtitle: Functions the integral builds from scratch
sections.body:
Some functions are DEFINED as accumulation integrals because no simpler formula exists. The premier example is the natural logarithm, constructible as ln(x) = ∫₁ˣ (1/t) dt: FTC1 instantly gives d/dx ln x = 1/x, and the log's properties (ln(ab) = ln a + ln b) can be derived from integral algebra. What Unit 2 asserted, the integral constructs.

Statistics runs on another: the error function erf(x) accumulates the bell curve e^{-t²}, which has no elementary antiderivative. Fresnel integrals (sin(t²)) drive optics. These functions are not exotic — they are what accumulation produces when the integrand resists closed forms, and FTC1 supplies their derivatives, their increasing/decreasing analysis, and (in Unit 10) their Taylor series — their entire calculus, formula-free.

For the AP, the operational point: a function presented as g(x) = 3 + ∫₂ˣ f(t) dt is a complete, analyzable object. Its value at 2 is 3 (the integral vanishes); its derivative is f; its tangent line at x = 2 is y = 3 + f(2)(x - 2). Initial value plus accumulated change — the chapter-1 sentence — IS this presentation, and FRQs phrase real models this way constantly.

The theorem's two halves are about to meet: Part 1 says accumulation functions are antiderivatives of their integrands. Part 2 (next chapter) runs the logic backward — ANY antiderivative, however obtained, evaluates the definite integral by subtraction. Together they collapse area computation from rectangle limits to algebra, and the unit's remaining chapters are the craft of finding antiderivatives.
key_terms: ln, erf, Fresnel — built by accumulation when formulas don't exist
g = C + ∫ₐˣ f: value, derivative, tangent, behavior — all readable
Accumulations are antiderivatives; Part 2 turns antiderivatives into evaluations
boxes: ap_alert

g(x) = 5 + ∫₃ˣ f(t) dt has g(3) = 5 — the integral from 3 to 3 is zero, leaving the constant. The 'find g at the anchor point' question is a freebie hidden in nearly every accumulation FRQ; collect it in five seconds.

mcq.question: If g(x) = ∫₁ˣ √(t³ + 1) dt, then g'(2) =

choices.C: Both A and B (they are equal)
choices.D: Cannot be determined without an antiderivative

mcq.explanation: FTC1: g'(x) = √(x³ + 1), so g'(2) = √9 = 3. No antiderivative needed — that is the theorem's point.

mcq.question: d/dx ∫₀^{x³} cos(t) dt =
mcq.explanation: Substitute the bound, multiply by its derivative: cos(x³)·3x². Choice B dodges the chain-rule fee.

mcq.question: F(x) = ∫ₓ⁵ e^{t²} dt. Then F'(x) =
mcq.explanation: The variable bound is on the BOTTOM: flip the integral's sign first, so F' = -e^{x²}.

mcq.question: g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt where the graph of f crosses the x-axis from below to above at x = 4. At x = 4, g has
mcq.explanation: g' = f changes − to + at 4: the first derivative test gives a local min of g.

mcq.question: h(x) = 7 + ∫₂ˣ sin(t²) dt. The tangent line to h at x = 2 is
mcq.explanation: h(2) = 7 (empty integral) and h'(2) = sin(4) by FTC1: point-slope assembles A.

frq.question:
The graph of f on [-2, 6] consists of line segments: from (-2, 2) to (0, 2), from (0, 2) to (2, -2), and from (2, -2) to (6, 2) — crossing zero at x = 1 and x = 4. Let g(x) = ∫₀ˣ f(t) dt.
(a) Compute g(-2), g(1), and g(4).
(b) Find the x-coordinates of all local extremes of g on (-2, 6) and classify them, citing the theorem that licenses your reasoning.
(c) On what interval(s) is g concave up? Justify.
rubric: (b) g' = f by FTC1; f: + on (-2,1), − on (1,4), + on (4,6): local max at x = 1, local min at x = 4
(c) g'' = f': f increasing on (2, 6) — g concave up there
Justifications cite g' = f and the sign changes
frq.model_answer: (a) g(1): triangle from 0 to 1 under the descending segment — f falls from 2 at x=0 to 0 at x=1: area ½(1)(2) = 1, so g(1) = 1. g(4) = g(1) + ∫₁⁴ f: the below-axis triangle from 1 to 4 has area ½(3)(2) = 3, so g(4) = 1 - 3 = -2. g(-2) = ∫₀⁻² f = -∫₋₂⁰ f = -(2·2) = -4 (rectangle of height 2, width 2, reversed bounds). (b) By the Fundamental Theorem, g'(x) = f(x). f changes from + to − at x = 1 (local maximum of g) and from − to + at x = 4 (local minimum of g). (c) g''(x) = f'(x): f is increasing on (2, 6) (the rising segment), so g is concave up on (2, 6).

frq.question:
Let F(x) = ∫₁^{x²} (ln t)/t dt for x > 1.
(a) Find F'(x), showing the chain-rule structure, and simplify using ln(x²) = 2 ln x.
(b) Solve F'(x) = 0 on the domain and explain what the result tells you about F.
(c) Compute F''(x) and determine the concavity of F for x > 1.
rubric: (a) F'(x) = (ln(x²)/x²)·2x, then ln(x²) = 2 ln x simplifies it to 4 ln x/x
(b) F' = 4 ln x/x = 0 only at ln x = 0, x = 1 (boundary); F' > 0 for x > 1: F strictly increasing
(c) F'' = 4(1 - ln x)/x²: positive on (1, e), negative on (e, ∞)
Concave up on (1, e), down on (e, ∞), inflection at x = e
frq.model_answer: (a) FTC1 with chain rule, u = x²: F'(x) = (ln(x²)/x²)·2x. Since ln(x²) = 2 ln x, this simplifies to F'(x) = (2 ln x/x²)(2x) = 4 ln x/x. (b) F'(x) = 4 ln x/x = 0 requires ln x = 0, i.e., x = 1 — the domain's edge. For all x > 1, ln x > 0 so F' > 0: F is strictly increasing on its whole domain, with no interior critical points. (c) F''(x) = 4·(x·(1/x) - ln x)/x² = 4(1 - ln x)/x². Positive when ln x < 1 (x < e), negative when x > e: F is concave up on (1, e), concave down on (e, ∞), with an inflection at x = e.

frq.question:
A reservoir's inflow rate is f(t) (acre-feet per day), graphed for 0 ≤ t ≤ 12: f is positive on (0, 5), negative on (5, 9), positive on (9, 12), with ∫₀⁵ f = 40, ∫₅⁹ f = -25, ∫₉¹² f = 10. The reservoir holds A(t) = 100 + ∫₀ᵗ f(s) ds acre-feet.
(a) Compute A(0), A(5), A(9), and A(12).
(b) When is the reservoir's volume greatest, and what is that volume? Justify via A' and the candidates comparison.
(c) The local water authority claims the reservoir never dropped below 110 acre-feet during the 12 days. Evaluate the claim.
rubric: (b) A' = f: + on (0,5), − on (5,9), + on (9,12); candidates t = 5 (max from sign change) vs endpoint t = 12: A(5) = 140 > 125
Greatest volume 140 acre-feet at t = 5
(c) Minimum candidates: t = 0 (100) and t = 9 (115); A(0) = 100 < 110 — claim false at the start
frq.model_answer: (a) A(0) = 100. A(5) = 100 + 40 = 140. A(9) = 140 - 25 = 115. A(12) = 115 + 10 = 125. (b) A'(t) = f(t) by the Fundamental Theorem. A rises on (0, 5), falls on (5, 9), rises on (9, 12) — local max at t = 5. Comparing with the right endpoint: A(5) = 140 versus A(12) = 125: the reservoir is fullest at t = 5 with 140 acre-feet. (c) The volume's minimum candidates are the left endpoint and the − to + turn at t = 9: A(0) = 100 and A(9) = 115. Since A(0) = 100 < 110, the claim is false — though only barely, and only at the very start: from the moment inflow began, the reservoir stayed above 110 after recovering past it early in the window. More precisely, A starts at 100, so 'never below 110' fails at t = 0 itself.

subject: AP Calculus BC
chapter_title: The Fundamental Theorem of Calculus — Part 2 and Antiderivatives
hook: Part 2 is the payoff: to evaluate any definite integral, find an antiderivative, plug in the endpoints, subtract. Centuries of area problems collapse into algebra — provided you can run differentiation backward, which is this chapter's craft.
learning_objectives: State and apply FTC Part 2: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) - F(a) for any antiderivative F
Build the basic antiderivative library by reversing the derivative rules
Use the +C correctly in indefinite integrals and drop it correctly in definite ones
Evaluate definite integrals of polynomials, powers, trig, exponentials, and 1/x
Solve initial-value problems: recover f from f' and a point

sections.title: Part 2 and the Evaluation Ritual
sections.subtitle: F(b) minus F(a)
sections.body:
FTC Part 2: if F is ANY antiderivative of the continuous function f (meaning F' = f), then ∫ₐᵇ f(x) dx = F(b) - F(a). The notation [F(x)]ₐᵇ packages the ritual: antidifferentiate, evaluate at the top, evaluate at the bottom, subtract. The connection to Part 1: the accumulation ∫ₐˣ f IS an antiderivative, and any two antiderivatives differ by a constant that cancels in the subtraction — so any antiderivative works.

The ritual, run: ∫₁³ x² dx = [x³/3]₁³ = 27/3 - 1/3 = 26/3. The rectangle limits of chapter 2 would labor for this; the algebra takes one line. That collapse — geometry into algebra — is why the theorem carries the name Fundamental.

Why no +C in definite integrals: include it and watch it cancel — (F(b) + C) - (F(a) + C) = F(b) - F(a). The constant is genuine bookkeeping for INDEFINITE integrals (next section) and pure decoration in definite ones. Writing it in definite evaluations is harmless but signals confusion; omitting it in indefinite answers loses a point.

Sign discipline in the subtraction: F(b) - F(a) with the TOP bound first, and parentheses around negative evaluations — ∫₋₂¹ x³ dx = [x⁴/4] = 1/4 - 16/4 = -15/4, where sloppy minus-handling routinely flips answers. The evaluation bar is the unit's highest-volume arithmetic; protect it with parentheses.
key_terms: ∫ₐᵇ f = F(b) - F(a) for any F with F' = f
Any antiderivative works — the +C dies in the subtraction
boxes: ap_alert

Calculator-section integrals can be evaluated numerically — but the no-calculator section's definite integrals are exactly this ritual, and arithmetic slips in F(b) - F(a) (especially with negative bounds and even powers) outnumber concept errors three to one. Parentheses around every substituted value.

sections.title: The Antiderivative Library
sections.subtitle: Differentiation's table, reversed
sections.body:
Every derivative fact reads backward as an antiderivative fact. The power rule reverses to ∫xⁿ dx = xⁿ⁺¹/(n + 1) + C for n ≠ -1 — raise the power, divide by the new power. The excluded case n = -1 is the logarithm's seat: ∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C, the absolute value extending the formula to negative x (where 1/x still demands an antiderivative and ln|x| supplies it).

Trig reverses with signs to mind: ∫cos = sin + C; ∫sin = -cos + C (the minus, because (cos)' = -sin); ∫sec² = tan + C; ∫sec·tan = sec + C; ∫csc² = -cot + C; ∫csc·cot = -csc + C. Exponentials: ∫eˣ = eˣ + C; ∫bˣ = bˣ/ln b + C. The inverse-trig pair from Unit 3, now in their destined role: ∫dx/(1 + x²) = arctan x + C and ∫dx/√(1 - x²) = arcsin x + C.

Linearity carries over wholesale: antidifferentiate term by term, constants ride along. ∫(6x² - 4 sin x + 5/x) dx = 2x³ + 4 cos x + 5 ln|x| + C — one C suffices for the whole expression (the constants merge). Rewriting before integrating is the same discipline as differentiating: √x → x^{1/2} → (2/3)x^{3/2}, and 1/x⁴ → x⁻⁴ → -x⁻³/3.

Verification is uniquely cheap in this direction: DIFFERENTIATE your answer and watch for the integrand. Antidifferentiation guesses are self-grading — a ten-second derivative check converts uncertainty into proof, and the habit catches sign slips (the ∫sin minus!) before they cost.
key_terms: ∫xⁿ = xⁿ⁺¹/(n+1) + C, n ≠ -1; the gap at -1 belongs to ln|x|
∫sin = -cos + C: antiderivative signs flip where derivative signs flipped
Check every antiderivative by differentiating it — self-grading work
boxes: ap_alert

∫(1/x) dx = ln|x| + C — the absolute value is graded on the AP. Omitting it on integrals whose interval is positive is tolerated; omitting it in general answers or on intervals touching negatives is a deduction. Write |x| by default.

sections.title: Initial Value Problems
sections.subtitle: Pinning down the +C
sections.body:
The indefinite integral's +C encodes a family: all vertical shifts of one antiderivative. An INITIAL CONDITION — one known point — selects the family member. Given f'(x) = 3x² - 4 with f(1) = 5: antidifferentiate to f(x) = x³ - 4x + C, substitute the point: 5 = 1 - 4 + C, so C = 8 and f(x) = x³ - 4x + 8. Antidifferentiate, substitute, solve, write the finished function — the four-beat IVP ritual.

Motion is the genre's home turf: given acceleration a(t) = -32 ft/s² (gravity), v(0) = 64, s(0) = 80 — antidifferentiate twice, pinning a constant at each level. v(t) = -32t + C₁ with v(0) = 64: v = -32t + 64. s(t) = -16t² + 64t + C₂ with s(0) = 80: s = -16t² + 64t + 80. Projectile problems, fully armed: when does it peak (v = 0), how high (s there), when does it land (s = 0).

The FTC alternative phrasing — f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' — solves IVPs without naming C: f(3) = f(1) + ∫₁³ (3x² - 4) dx = 5 + [x³ - 4x]₁³ = 5 + (15 - (-3)) = 23. When only ONE value is wanted (not the whole formula), the accumulation route is faster and calculator-friendly; when the formula is wanted, the C-route delivers it. Both phrasings are the same mathematics; fluency means choosing by what the question requests.

Two-constant problems flag a BC reflex: each antidifferentiation level needs its own condition, and conditions can arrive at different points (v(2) = 10, s(0) = 3) — substitute each at ITS point, in order. The bookkeeping is trivial when organized level by level and a mess when interleaved.
key_terms: f' plus one point determines f: antidifferentiate, substitute, solve for C
a → v → s, one constant pinned per level
f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f': the C-free route to single values
boxes: ap_alert

When an FRQ gives f' and f(a) and asks only for f(b), skip the C entirely: f(b) = f(a) + ∫ₐᵇ f' dx, evaluated (by hand or calculator as the section permits). The accumulation route is faster, C-error-proof, and worth the same full credit.

sections.title: Hypotheses and Honest Limits
sections.subtitle: Where Part 2 can fail, and graph-based evaluation
sections.body:
Part 2's hypothesis — f continuous on [a, b] — is not decoration. The cautionary classic: ∫₋₁¹ (1/x²) dx 'evaluated' as [-1/x]₋₁¹ = -1 - 1 = -2. A negative area for a positive function: absurd. The failure: 1/x² is discontinuous (unbounded) at 0, inside the interval; the theorem never applied, and the integral is in fact improper (chapter 8's subject) and divergent. Scan the interval for discontinuities BEFORE invoking the ritual.

Piecewise integrands route around their seams by splitting: ∫₀⁴ f with f defined piecewise at x = 2 becomes ∫₀² + ∫₂⁴, each piece evaluated by its own formula. Absolute-value integrands are the recurring case: for ∫₀⁴ |x - 2| dx, split at the corner x = 2: ∫₀² (2 - x) dx + ∫₂⁴ (x - 2) dx = 2 + 2 = 4. Splitting at the kink converts one impossible antiderivative into two trivial ones.

When no elementary antiderivative exists (e^{-x²}, sin(x²), the unit's recurring guests), Part 2 is not wrong but UNAVAILABLE — evaluation falls back to geometry (chapter 1), numerics (chapter 2), the calculator (on active sections), or stays symbolic as an accumulation function (chapter 3). Knowing WHICH tool a given integral admits is itself the tested skill: the exam mixes evaluable and non-evaluable integrands deliberately.

The unit's arc from here: the library handles integrands that LOOK like derivative-table entries. Most integrands don't — they look like chain-rule outputs (u-substitution, next), product-rule outputs (integration by parts), or rational functions (partial fractions). The remaining chapters are pattern-recognition training: which derivative rule, run backward, unlocks each integrand family.
key_terms: Discontinuities inside [a, b] void the ritual — check before evaluating
Piecewise and absolute-value integrands integrate piece by piece
Geometry, numerics, FTC, or symbolic accumulation — matched to the integrand
boxes: ap_alert

∫|expression| dx ALWAYS splits at the expression's zeros — there is no antiderivative of an absolute value in one piece. The split-point computation is the question's actual content; the two resulting integrals are routine.

Evaluate the following, showing antiderivatives and the evaluation bar.
(a) ∫₁⁸ 3·x^{1/3} dx
(b) ∫_{π/4}^{π/2} (2 cos x - csc² x) dx

frq.question:
A ball is thrown upward from a 96-foot building with initial velocity 16 ft/s; acceleration is a(t) = -32 ft/s².
(a) Find v(t) and s(t).
(b) Find the maximum height, with justification that it is a maximum.
(c) Find the speed at the moment of impact with the ground.
rubric: (b) v = 0 at t = ½; s(½) = -4 + 8 + 96 = 100 ft; v changes + to − (or s'' < 0): maximum
Speed |v(3)| = 80 ft/s
frq.model_answer: (a) v(t) = ∫a dt = -32t + C₁ with v(0) = 16: v(t) = -32t + 16. s(t) = ∫v dt = -16t² + 16t + C₂ with s(0) = 96: s(t) = -16t² + 16t + 96. (b) v(t) = 0 at t = ½ s. v changes from positive to negative there (linear with negative slope), so s has its maximum: s(½) = -4 + 8 + 96 = 100 feet. (c) Impact: s(t) = 0 ⟹ -16(t² - t - 6) = 0 ⟹ (t - 3)(t + 2) = 0 ⟹ t = 3 s. v(3) = -96 + 16 = -80 ft/s — moving downward at impact, with speed |−80| = 80 ft/s.

frq.question:
Let f be continuous with f(2) = 7, and suppose f'(x) = 6x² - 10x for all x.
(a) Find f(x) using an initial value computation.
(b) Recompute f(4) using the accumulation form f(4) = f(2) + ∫₂⁴ f'(x) dx, and confirm the two routes agree.
(c) Explain why the two routes must always agree, referencing the appropriate part of the Fundamental Theorem.
rubric: Direct check: f(4) = 128 - 80 + 11 = 59 ✓
(c) FTC Part 2: ∫₂⁴ f' = f(4) - f(2) for any antiderivative — the accumulation IS the net change
frq.model_answer: (a) f(x) = 2x³ - 5x² + C. The condition: 7 = 2(8) - 5(4) + C = -4 + C, so C = 11 and f(x) = 2x³ - 5x² + 11. (b) ∫₂⁴ (6x² - 10x) dx = [2x³ - 5x²]₂⁴ = (128 - 80) - (16 - 20) = 48 - (-4) = 52. So f(4) = 7 + 52 = 59. Direct: f(4) = 128 - 80 + 11 = 59 ✓. (c) FTC Part 2 states ∫₂⁴ f'(x) dx = f(4) - f(2) — the definite integral of a rate is exactly the net change of the function. Adding f(2) to both sides gives the accumulation form, so the C-route and the accumulation route are algebraic rearrangements of the same theorem; they cannot disagree.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: Most integrands aren't in the library — they're chain-rule outputs wearing disguises. u-Substitution is the chain rule run backward: spot the inside function, watch its derivative cancel, and a hopeless integral becomes a one-line lookup.
learning_objectives: Identify integrands of the form f(g(x))·g'(x) suitable for substitution
Execute the substitution ritual: choose u, compute du, rewrite, integrate, back-substitute
Change the bounds of definite integrals to u-values and never return to x
Handle constant-adjustment substitutions where du differs by a factor
Recognize the ln|u| pattern for integrands shaped like u'/u

sections.title: The Chain Rule, Reversed
sections.subtitle: Spotting the inside function
sections.body:
Differentiating F(g(x)) produces f(g(x))·g'(x) — a composition times the inside's derivative. So any integrand with that anatomy antidifferentiates by recognizing it: ∫f(g(x))·g'(x) dx = F(g(x)) + C. u-Substitution mechanizes the recognition: set u = g(x), compute du = g'(x) dx, and the integral REWRITES as ∫f(u) du — a library problem in the u-world.

The showcase: ∫2x(x² + 3)⁴ dx. The inside is x² + 3; its derivative 2x sits right there as a factor. Let u = x² + 3, du = 2x dx: the integral becomes ∫u⁴ du = u⁵/5 + C = (x² + 3)⁵/5 + C. Differentiate to verify: 5·(x²+3)⁴/5 · 2x ✓ — the chain rule regenerates the integrand, confirming the whole philosophy.

What to choose as u: the INSIDE of the composition — the expression under a power, inside a trig function, in an exponent, under a root. The litmus test: after computing du, the REST of the integrand should disappear into it. If x-stuff survives the substitution, the choice failed; pick again or suspect another technique.

The dx is not decoration: du = g'(x) dx is a complete package (the differentials from Unit 4's linearization chapter, earning their keep), and every x and dx must convert to u and du before integrating. A half-converted integral — u's and x's cohabiting — is meaningless and ungradable; the rewrite is all-or-nothing.
key_terms: Set u = inside, du = u' dx; rewrite wholly in u; integrate; back-substitute
f(g(x))·g'(x): composition present, inside's derivative available as a factor
No x may survive into the u-integral — mixed-variable integrals are meaningless
boxes: ap_alert

Choose u so that du is VISIBLY waiting in the integrand: in ∫x e^{x²} dx, u = x² works because du = 2x dx matches the loose x (up to the constant 2). If no candidate u has its derivative on site, u-substitution is the wrong tool — move on.

sections.title: Constant Adjustment
sections.subtitle: When du is off by a factor
sections.body:
Usually the integrand carries ALMOST du: ∫x e^{x²} dx has u = x², du = 2x dx, but only x dx appears — half of du. Constants are no obstacle: x dx = du/2, so the integral is ∫e^u (du/2) = e^u/2 + C = e^{x²}/2 + C. Solve du's equation for the piece you actually have, and the constant rides outside.

The canonical small cases live here: ∫cos(3x) dx with u = 3x gives sin(3x)/3 + C; ∫e^{5x} dx = e^{5x}/5 + C; ∫(2x + 7)⁹ dx = (2x + 7)¹⁰/20 + C. Linear insides ax + b always cost a factor of 1/a — a pattern worth automating since it covers a third of all exam substitutions.

What constant adjustment can NEVER do: manufacture missing VARIABLES. ∫e^{x²} dx (no loose x) does not yield to u = x² — du = 2x dx demands an x the integrand lacks, and no constant fixes a missing variable. That integral has no elementary antiderivative at all; recognizing the difference between off-by-a-constant (fixable) and off-by-a-variable (fatal) is a graded discrimination.

The u'/u pattern deserves its own reflex: any integrand shaped like derivative-over-function integrates to ln|function|. ∫x/(x² + 1) dx: u = x² + 1 catches du = 2x dx, giving ½ln(x² + 1) + C. ∫tan x dx = ∫sin x/cos x dx with u = cos x: -ln|cos x| + C = ln|sec x| + C — the tangent integral, derived in one substitution and worth memorizing as a result.
key_terms: x dx = du/2 and friends — solve du's equation for what you have
Derivative-over-function integrates to ln of the function — tan x's secret
boxes: ap_alert

Constants adjust; variables don't. ∫x e^{x²} dx submits to u-substitution, ∫e^{x²} dx does not — and the exam pairs them deliberately. The presence or absence of the loose x is the entire question; check it before committing.

sections.title: Definite Integrals: Change the Bounds
sections.subtitle: Move to u-world and stay there
sections.body:
For definite integrals, convert the BOUNDS along with everything else: when u = g(x), the x-bounds a, b become u-bounds g(a), g(b), and the evaluation finishes entirely in u. ∫₀² x√(x² + 1) dx: u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx; bounds x = 0 → u = 1, x = 2 → u = 5. The integral is ½∫₁⁵ √u du = ½·(2/3)u^{3/2}|₁⁵ = (5√5 - 1)/3. No back-substitution, no returning to x — the bounds did the conversion permanently.

The alternative — keeping x-bounds, back-substituting, then evaluating — is legal but slower and traps the unwary who plug x-values into u-expressions. The AP convention rewards bound-changing: write the new bounds ON the integral sign at the rewrite step, and the work self-documents. Mixed notation (u-integrand with x-bounds) is ambiguous and costs presentation points.

Bound order can FLIP under decreasing substitutions: u = cos x on [0, π/2] sends the bounds to 1 and 0 — the u-integral runs from 1 to 0, and reversing it (with the sign flip from chapter 1's properties) tidies the evaluation. The flip is not an error; it is the substitution being honest about direction. ∫₀^{π/2} sin x cos⁴x dx: u = cos x, du = -sin x dx: -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = 1/5.

Symmetry dividends arrive free in u-world: substitutions sometimes reveal that a definite integral's u-version has equal bounds (instant zero) or symmetric bounds with an odd integrand (also zero). The bounds carry information; converting them early lets that information surface before any antiderivative work.
key_terms: x-bounds map through u = g(x): evaluate wholly in u-world
New bounds written on the integral at the substitution step
Decreasing u reverses bound order; the sign-flip property restores it
boxes: ap_alert

The classic definite-substitution error: rewriting ∫₀² ... dx as ∫ u⁴ du and then evaluating at 0 and 2 — the OLD x-bounds — in the u-antiderivative. Changing the bounds at the moment of substitution makes the error structurally impossible. Change them every time.

sections.title: Substitution Judgment
sections.subtitle: Recognition drills and rearrangement tricks
sections.body:
Fluency is recognizing the family fast. Powers of an inside: (x³ + 1)⁷·x² dx — u = x³ + 1. Exponentials of an inside: e^{sin x}cos x dx — u = sin x. Roots of an inside: x√(x² - 4) — u = x² - 4. Trig of an inside: sec²(5x) — linear inside. Derivative-over-function: (2x + 3)/(x² + 3x) — u'/u, instant logarithm. Five patterns cover the AP's substitution menu nearly completely.

The rearrangement trick for stubborn leftovers: ∫x√(x - 1) dx with u = x - 1 leaves a loose x — but x = u + 1 converts it: ∫(u + 1)√u du = ∫(u^{3/2} + u^{1/2}) du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C, back-substituted. When u's equation can be SOLVED for the leftover x, the substitution survives; this 'back-solve' extension handles the linear-inside-with-extra-x family the exam likes.

When substitution fails, the diagnosis matters: a PRODUCT of unrelated functions (x·sin x — no composition anywhere) signals integration by parts, next chapter. A RATIONAL function with factorable denominator signals partial fractions, the chapter after. The techniques partition the integrand world; mis-routing wastes minutes, and the routing cue is structural (composition? product? ratio?) exactly like Unit 3's dispatch algorithm for derivatives.

Verification stays cheap: differentiate the answer. Every substitution result, indefinite or definite-by-antiderivative, self-checks in ten seconds via the chain rule — which is, after all, what u-substitution was the whole time.
key_terms: Power, exponential, root, trig of an inside, plus u'/u — the recognition set
Leftover x converts via x = (solve u's equation): handles x√(x-1)
Composition → substitution; bare product → parts; factorable ratio → partial fractions
boxes: ap_alert

Five-second routing scan before integrating anything: is there a composition with its inside's derivative nearby (u-sub)? A product of unrelated pieces (parts)? A rational function (partial fractions or u'/u)? The scan assigns the tool; tools misassigned cost double time.

frq.question:
Evaluate each integral, showing the substitution, the du equation, and (where definite) the converted bounds.
(a) ∫ sec²(4x) dx
(b) ∫₀^{π/2} sin x cos⁴x dx
(c) ∫₁² x/(x² + 1) dx
rubric: (a) u = 4x: tan(4x)/4 + C
(b) u = cos x, du = -sin x dx, bounds 1 → 0; -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = 1/5
(c) u = x² + 1, bounds 2 → 5: ½∫₂⁵ du/u = ½(ln 5 - ln 2) = ½ln(5/2)
Bounds converted at the substitution step in (b) and (c)
frq.model_answer: (a) u = 4x, du = 4 dx: ∫sec²u (du/4) = tan(u)/4 + C = tan(4x)/4 + C. (b) u = cos x, du = -sin x dx; bounds: x = 0 → u = 1, x = π/2 → u = 0. The integral becomes -∫₁⁰ u⁴ du = ∫₀¹ u⁴ du = [u⁵/5]₀¹ = 1/5. (c) u = x² + 1, du = 2x dx; bounds: x = 1 → u = 2, x = 2 → u = 5. The integral is ½∫₂⁵ du/u = ½[ln u]₂⁵ = ½(ln 5 - ln 2) = ½ ln(5/2).

frq.question:
Consider ∫ x√(x - 1) dx.
(a) Explain why the naive substitution u = x - 1 appears to fail, and how the back-solve x = u + 1 rescues it.
(b) Complete the integration.
(c) Verify your answer by differentiation.
rubric: (a) u = x - 1 leaves a loose x; since x = u + 1, the leftover converts exactly
(b) ∫(u + 1)u^{1/2} du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C, back-substituted with u = x - 1
Factoring step in the verification shown
frq.model_answer: (a) With u = x - 1, du = dx, but the integrand keeps a factor of x not covered by du — normally fatal. However, u's equation solves for it: x = u + 1, converting every leftover. (b) ∫(u + 1)√u du = ∫(u^{3/2} + u^{1/2}) du = (2/5)u^{5/2} + (2/3)u^{3/2} + C = (2/5)(x-1)^{5/2} + (2/3)(x-1)^{3/2} + C. (c) Differentiating: (x-1)^{3/2} + (x-1)^{1/2}. Factor out (x-1)^{1/2}: (x-1)^{1/2}[(x-1) + 1] = x(x-1)^{1/2} = x√(x-1) ✓ — the original integrand.

frq.question:
The rate of oil leakage from a tanker is R(t) = 50t e^{-t²/8} liters per hour, t in hours.
(a) Find the total oil leaked from t = 0 to t = 2 using a substitution with converted bounds.
(b) Find the time at which the leakage RATE is greatest, using Unit 5 machinery on R.
(c) Total leakage over all time would be ∫₀^∞ R dt — name the chapter-ahead concept this integral requires, and explain in one sentence why the bound ∞ demands new machinery.
rubric: (b) R' = 50e^{-t²/8}(1 - t²/4) = 0 → t = 2; sign change + to −: maximum at t = 2
(c) Improper integral
Reason: ∞ is not a number to substitute — the integral is defined as a limit of finite-bound integrals
frq.model_answer: (a) Let u = t²/8, du = (t/4) dt, so t dt = 4 du; bounds t = 0 → u = 0, t = 2 → u = 1/2. ∫₀² 50 t e^{-t²/8} dt = 50·4∫₀^{1/2} e^{-u} du = 200[-e^{-u}]₀^{1/2} = 200(1 - e^{-1/2}) ≈ 78.7 liters. (b) R'(t) = 50e^{-t²/8} + 50t·e^{-t²/8}·(-t/4) = 50e^{-t²/8}(1 - t²/4). The exponential never vanishes; 1 - t²/4 = 0 at t = 2, with R' changing + to − there: the leak rate peaks at t = 2 hours. (c) ∫₀^∞ R dt is an IMPROPER integral. Infinity is not a number that can be substituted into an antiderivative — the integral must be defined as lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ R dt, the limit machinery of this unit's final chapter.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY — and worth the price of admission: integration by parts is the product rule run backward, the only tool that integrates x·eˣ, x·cos x, and ln x itself. One formula, one choosing-rule, and a whole family of integrals falls.
learning_objectives: Derive the parts formula ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du from the product rule
Choose u by the LIATE priority and dv as the rest
Apply parts iteratively for powers like x² eˣ
Integrate ln x and other lone awkward functions via dv = dx
Execute the boundary-term bookkeeping for definite integrals

sections.title: The Product Rule, Reversed
sections.subtitle: Deriving ∫u dv = uv − ∫v du
sections.body:
Integrate the product rule (uv)' = u'v + uv' across an interval: uv = ∫u'v + ∫uv'. Rearranged: ∫u v' dx = uv - ∫u' v dx, or in differential shorthand, ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du. Integration by parts trades one integral for another — and the entire craft is making the trade FAVORABLE: ∫v du should be simpler than ∫u dv.

The showcase: ∫x eˣ dx. Choose u = x (differentiates to the simpler 1) and dv = eˣ dx (integrates without getting worse, to v = eˣ). The formula: ∫x eˣ dx = x eˣ - ∫eˣ·1 dx = x eˣ - eˣ + C = (x - 1)eˣ + C. The x DIED under differentiation — that is the trade working: polynomial factors are mortal, and parts kills them one differentiation at a time.

The bookkeeping layout that prevents chaos: a 2×2 box — u and dv on top, du and v below — filled before touching the formula. u = x, dv = eˣ dx; du = dx, v = eˣ. Then transcribe: uv minus the integral of v du. The box is to parts what the skeleton was to the quotient rule: structure that survives exam pressure.

No +C appears when computing v from dv — any antiderivative works (the constant would cancel through the formula, same argument as FTC2), so take the cleanest one. The final answer carries one +C, attached at the end.
key_terms: ∫u dv = uv - ∫v du: the product rule integrated and rearranged
Choose so ∫v du is SIMPLER — typically u dies under differentiation
u, dv / du, v — filled completely before invoking the formula
boxes: ap_alert

Parts is BC-only material and the exam flags it with unmistakable integrands: x eˣ, x sin x, x ln x, ln x alone, arctan x alone. Polynomial-times-transcendental is the silhouette; when you see it, draw the box.

sections.title: Choosing u: LIATE
sections.subtitle: The priority list that almost never fails
sections.body:
The choice of u decides everything, and the LIATE mnemonic ranks candidates: Logarithmic, Inverse trig, Algebraic (polynomials), Trigonometric, Exponential — choose u as the EARLIEST type present; dv swallows the rest. Logs and inverse trig differentiate beautifully (to algebraic functions) but integrate painfully, so they grab u; exponentials integrate without complaint, so they accept dv.

Run the list: ∫x cos x dx — Algebraic beats Trig: u = x, dv = cos x dx, giving x sin x - ∫sin x dx = x sin x + cos x + C. ∫x ln x dx — Log beats Algebraic: u = ln x, dv = x dx: (x²/2)ln x - ∫(x²/2)(1/x) dx = (x²/2)ln x - x²/4 + C. The ranking inverts naive instinct (the ln, not the x, takes u) and that inversion is exactly what LIATE encodes.

Why LIATE works, in one sentence: it orders functions from 'differentiates-much-simpler' to 'integrates-without-damage' — u wants the former, dv needs the latter. Understanding the principle lets you sanity-check the mnemonic on hybrids and trust departures from it in the rare cases (none on the AP) where it misleads.

The wrong choice diagnoses itself: picking u = eˣ in ∫x eˣ dx produces ∫v du = ∫(x²/2)eˣ dx — WORSE than the start. A trade that complicates is a signal to swap the roles, not to push harder. One failed box costs thirty seconds; recognizing the failure fast is part of the skill.
key_terms: Log, Inverse trig, Algebraic, Trig, Exponential — u takes the earliest type present
u should simplify under d/dx; dv must integrate without damage
If ∫v du is worse than the original, swap the choice and rerun
boxes: ap_alert

∫ln x dx — a lone logarithm — is the LIATE edge case the exam loves: u = ln x and dv = dx (yes, just dx). Then v = x and the formula gives x ln x - ∫x·(1/x) dx = x ln x - x + C. The dv = dx move also integrates arctan x; memorize the maneuver.

sections.title: Iteration and the Definite Version
sections.subtitle: Higher powers, boundary terms
sections.body:
Powers above one need repeated parts: ∫x² eˣ dx with u = x² gives x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx — the remaining integral is last section's showcase, yielding x² eˣ - 2(x - 1)eˣ + C = (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C. Each round kills one power; xⁿ needs n rounds. The discipline: keep LIATE's choice (algebraic stays u) consistent through every round — swapping mid-stream undoes the previous round's progress exactly.

Definite integrals carry the boundary term through: ∫ₐᵇ u dv = [uv]ₐᵇ - ∫ₐᵇ v du. The uv piece evaluates at the bounds IMMEDIATELY — it is a number — while the remaining integral proceeds. ∫₁ᵉ ln x dx = [x ln x]₁ᵉ - ∫₁ᵉ dx = (e·1 - 1·0) - (e - 1) = e - e + 1 = 1. A clean, exam-loved result: the area under ln from 1 to e is exactly 1.

The circular family closes the chapter's technique list: ∫eˣ sin x dx runs parts twice (either consistent choice) and reproduces ITSELF: ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ sin x - eˣ cos x - ∫eˣ sin x dx. The escape move: add the integral to both sides and divide by 2 — ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ(sin x - cos x)/2 + C. The 'solve for the integral' finale turns apparent circularity into the answer; it appears on BC exams as the hardest parts variant.

Tabular shorthand for the iterative cases: columns of repeated derivatives of u (down to zero) and repeated antiderivatives of dv, joined diagonally with alternating signs. For x² eˣ: derivatives x², 2x, 2, 0; antiderivatives eˣ, eˣ, eˣ; diagonals (+x²eˣ)(-2xeˣ)(+2eˣ) — the answer assembled without writing the formula once. Legal, fast, and self-checking against the longhand.
key_terms: xⁿ dies in n rounds; keep the LIATE roles fixed throughout
[uv]ₐᵇ evaluates immediately; only ∫v du continues as an integral
eˣ sin x: two rounds reproduce the integral — add and divide by 2
boxes: ap_alert

In the circular eˣ·trig cases, the second round must keep the SAME choice pattern as the first (exponential as dv both times, or trig as dv both times) — mixing undoes round one and returns the original integral with nothing gained. Consistency is the entire trick.

sections.title: Parts in Context
sections.subtitle: Where the technique lives on the exam
sections.body:
Routing review, now three techniques deep: composition with inside's derivative → u-substitution; product of UNRELATED functions (no composition) → parts; lone awkward function (ln x, arctan x) → parts with dv = dx. The x e^{x²} versus x eˣ pair is the canonical discrimination: the first has the composition anatomy (substitution, instantly), the second is a genuine unrelated product (parts). Thirty seconds of routing beats five minutes of wrong-tool grinding.

Applied integrals deliver parts in costume: expected values in probability (∫x·f(x) dx with exponential densities), work and center-of-mass integrals, and BC's own coming attractions — arc-length and surface integrals occasionally reduce to parts-able forms, and Taylor series remainders (Unit 10) are proved with iterated parts. The technique is infrastructure, not trivia.

Accumulation-function problems hybridize with FTC: given F(x) = ∫₀ˣ t cos t dt, find F(π) — run parts inside the accumulation: [t sin t + cos t]₀^π = (0 + (-1)) - (0 + 1) = -2. The FTC supplies the frame; parts supplies the antiderivative; the layered problem is BC's bread and butter.

A final calibration note: parts problems on the AP stay SHALLOW — one round, occasionally two, the ln x maneuver, rarely the circular case. Triple iterations and exotic choices live in textbooks, not on the exam. Master the box, LIATE, the dv = dx move, and the boundary term; that inventory covers every parts question the AP has asked in a decade.
key_terms: Substitution (composition), parts (product), dv = dx (lone awkward function)
The discrimination pair: composition anatomy versus genuine product
One-to-two rounds, ln x, boundary terms — the complete AP inventory
boxes: ap_alert

Before starting any parts computation on a definite integral, check whether the integrand is secretly a u-substitution: ∫x e^{x²} dx submits to u = x² in one line, and running parts on it instead is a time-loss the exam engineers deliberately. Composition check first, always.
