frq.question:
Let I = ∫ x² eˣ dx.
(a) Set up the first round of integration by parts with the LIATE-correct choice, and carry it through to the reduced integral.
(b) Complete the second round and state the final antiderivative.
(c) Verify your answer by differentiation.
rubric: (a) u = x², dv = eˣ dx: I = x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx
(b) Second round on ∫x eˣ: (x - 1)eˣ; assembled: (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C
(c) Differentiates: (2x - 2)eˣ + (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ = x² eˣ ✓
Consistent u-choice across rounds
frq.model_answer: (a) LIATE: algebraic u = x², dv = eˣ dx; du = 2x dx, v = eˣ. I = x² eˣ - ∫eˣ·2x dx = x² eˣ - 2∫x eˣ dx. (b) For ∫x eˣ dx: u = x, dv = eˣ dx gives x eˣ - eˣ. So I = x² eˣ - 2(x eˣ - eˣ) + C = (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ + C. (c) d/dx[(x² - 2x + 2)eˣ] = (2x - 2)eˣ + (x² - 2x + 2)eˣ = (x² )eˣ = x² eˣ ✓.

frq.question:
Evaluate ∫₀^{π/2} x sin x dx.
(a) Run integration by parts with the boundary-term bookkeeping.
(b) Interpret the boundary term's value at each endpoint.
(c) A region under y = x sin x from 0 to π/2 is proposed as a machine part's cross-section. State its exact area from (a), and approximate it to three decimals.
rubric: (a) u = x, dv = sin x dx: [-x cos x]₀^{π/2} + ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx
Boundary term: 0 at both ends (cos(π/2) = 0; x = 0 at the bottom); remaining integral [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 1
(b) Top end dies via cos(π/2) = 0, bottom via the factor x = 0
(c) Area exactly 1; approximation 1.000
frq.model_answer: (a) u = x, dv = sin x dx; du = dx, v = -cos x. ∫₀^{π/2} x sin x dx = [-x cos x]₀^{π/2} + ∫₀^{π/2} cos x dx = (-（π/2)·0 + 0·1) + [sin x]₀^{π/2} = 0 + 1 = 1. (b) The boundary term vanishes at BOTH ends for different reasons: at x = π/2 because cos(π/2) = 0, and at x = 0 because the factor x itself is zero — a small bookkeeping elegance worth noticing. (c) The exact area is 1 square unit; to three decimals, 1.000.

frq.question:
Let J = ∫ eˣ cos x dx.
(a) Apply integration by parts twice with a consistent choice, showing that J reappears on the right side.
(b) Solve the resulting equation for J.
(c) Use your result to evaluate ∫₀^{π} eˣ cos x dx exactly.
rubric: (a) u = cos x both rounds (or eˣ both rounds): J = eˣ cos x + ∫eˣ sin x = eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x - J
(b) 2J = eˣ(cos x + sin x): J = eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2 + C
Consistency of choice across rounds stated
frq.model_answer: (a) Round 1: u = cos x, dv = eˣ dx: J = eˣ cos x + ∫eˣ sin x dx. Round 2 (same pattern, u = sin x): ∫eˣ sin x dx = eˣ sin x - ∫eˣ cos x dx = eˣ sin x - J. Substituting: J = eˣ cos x + eˣ sin x - J. (b) 2J = eˣ(sin x + cos x), so J = eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2 + C. (c) ∫₀^π eˣ cos x dx = [eˣ(sin x + cos x)/2]₀^π = (e^π(0 + (-1)))/2 - (1(0 + 1))/2 = -e^π/2 - 1/2 = -(e^π + 1)/2.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY: a rational function that refuses every substitution splits — like a fraction into ½ + ⅓ — into pieces that each integrate to a logarithm. Partial fractions is algebra in service of integration, and the AP keeps its version mercifully tame.
learning_objectives: Decompose rational functions with distinct linear factors into partial fractions
Find the constants by the cover-up (root-substitution) method
Integrate each piece to its logarithm and assemble the answer
Divide first when the rational function is improper (top degree ≥ bottom degree)
Recognize the AP's boundaries: nonrepeating linear factors only

sections.title: Splitting the Fraction
sections.subtitle: Why and how the decomposition exists
sections.body:
The integrand 1/((x - 1)(x + 2)) defeats u-substitution (no factor's derivative is present) and parts (no useful product) — but it SPLITS: 1/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2) for the right constants A and B. Each piece is a u'/u-style logarithm-in-waiting; the decomposition converts one impossible integral into two trivial ones.

Why such constants exist: combining A/(x - 1) + B/(x + 2) over the common denominator gives (A(x + 2) + B(x - 1))/((x - 1)(x + 2)) — a numerator that is a general linear polynomial with two adjustable constants, enough freedom to match any constant or linear numerator. Distinct linear factors downstairs, one constant per factor upstairs: the template.

Finding A and B by clearing denominators: 1 = A(x + 2) + B(x - 1), an identity holding for ALL x. Substituting the roots makes terms vanish: x = 1 kills B's term — 1 = 3A, A = 1/3; x = -2 kills A's: 1 = -3B, B = -1/3. The root-substitution shortcut (the 'cover-up method') finds each constant in one line: cover the factor in the original fraction, evaluate the remainder at that factor's root.

The integration finale: ∫dx/((x-1)(x+2)) = (1/3)∫dx/(x-1) - (1/3)∫dx/(x+2) = (1/3)ln|x-1| - (1/3)ln|x+2| + C = (1/3)ln|(x-1)/(x+2)| + C. Decompose, integrate each piece, optionally consolidate the logs. Three beats, every time.
key_terms: Distinct linear factors split: one constant over each factor
Each constant = the original fraction with its factor covered, evaluated at that root
Each piece is c/(x - r): integrates to c·ln|x - r|
boxes: ap_alert

BC's partial fractions stay tame by design: DISTINCT LINEAR factors only — no repeated factors, no irreducible quadratics. If your decomposition seems to need A/(x-1)² or (Bx + C)/(x² + 1), re-read the problem; the AP didn't ask that.

sections.title: The Cover-Up Method, Drilled
sections.subtitle: Constants in one line each
sections.body:
The cover-up method formalized: to find the constant over (x - r), delete ('cover') that factor from the original fraction's denominator and evaluate what remains at x = r. For (3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 3)): the constant over (x + 1) is (3x + 5)/(x + 3) at x = -1: 2/2 = 1; over (x + 3): (3x + 5)/(x + 1) at x = -3: -4/(-2) = 2. Decomposition: 1/(x + 1) + 2/(x + 3). Integral: ln|x + 1| + 2 ln|x + 3| + C.

Why it works is the clearing-denominators argument compressed: substituting the root into the cleared identity annihilates every term except the target constant's. The method is rigorous, not a trick — but verify once per exam anyway: recombine the pieces mentally (or check one x-value, like x = 0) to confirm the split. Thirty seconds, and decomposition errors die before they propagate into logarithms.

Three-factor versions scale linearly: (x + 7)/((x)(x - 2)(x + 1)) gets three constants, each by one cover-up. The arithmetic multiplies, the method doesn't change. The exam's appetite stops at two or three factors; beyond that is textbook territory.

Definite versions assemble bounds onto the logs: ∫₃⁵ dx/((x - 1)(x + 2)) = (1/3)[ln|x - 1| - ln|x + 2|]₃⁵ = (1/3)[(ln 4 - ln 7) - (ln 2 - ln 5)] = (1/3)ln(10/7) after log algebra. Exact-form answers with consolidated logarithms are the expected presentation — decimal conversions only when the question asks.
key_terms: Cover the factor, evaluate at its root — one constant per line
Recombine or spot-check one x-value before integrating
ln a - ln b = ln(a/b): definite answers compress to single logarithms
boxes: ap_alert

After the cover-up, sanity-check SIGNS by recombining the first terms mentally: A/(x-1) + B/(x+2) should reproduce the original numerator's sign at a glance. Sign slips in cover-up arithmetic are the technique's only common failure mode.

sections.title: Improper Fractions Divide First
sections.subtitle: When the top is too big
sections.body:
Partial fractions demands a PROPER rational function — numerator degree strictly below denominator degree. When the top matches or exceeds the bottom, polynomial long division goes first: (x² + 3x + 5)/((x + 1)(x + 2)) = (x² + 3x + 5)/(x² + 3x + 2) divides to 1 + 3/((x + 1)(x + 2)) — a polynomial part plus a proper remainder fraction, each integrable by its own rules.

The polynomial part integrates trivially; the remainder decomposes as usual: 3/((x+1)(x+2)) = 3/(x+1) - 3/(x+2). Total: x + 3 ln|x+1| - 3 ln|x+2| + C. Divide, decompose, integrate — the full pipeline for any rational function in the AP's scope.

The degree check must be a reflex: scan top and bottom degrees BEFORE writing any A/(x - r) template. Decomposing an improper fraction produces unsolvable constant equations or wrong answers that look plausible — the failure is quiet, which is what makes the upfront check mandatory. Top degree ≥ bottom degree: divide. Always.

A BC connection ahead: the logistic differential equation (Unit 7) separates into exactly a partial-fractions integral — ∫dP/(P(L - P)) — and this chapter's technique is what solves it. Partial fractions is not an isolated trick; it is the algebra inside BC's most famous differential equation, which is reason enough for its place in the course.
key_terms: Numerator degree < denominator degree, or divide first
∫dP/(P(L - P)) — Unit 7's star equation runs on this chapter
boxes: ap_alert

Degree check FIRST: (x²+1)/((x-1)(x+2)) has equal degrees (2 and 2) and must be divided before decomposing. The improper-fraction trap is quiet — the A/B template seems to work and yields a wrong answer with no alarm. Make the check muscle memory.

sections.title: Routing, Completed
sections.subtitle: The integration decision tree, four techniques deep
sections.body:
The unit's decision tree, now complete for AP purposes: (1) Library form? Integrate directly. (2) Composition with the inside's derivative present (up to a constant)? u-Substitution. (3) u'/u shape specifically? Instant logarithm. (4) Product of unrelated functions, or a lone log/inverse-trig? Parts. (5) Rational function? Check degrees (divide if improper), check the denominator (factorable into distinct linear pieces?), then partial fractions. (6) None of the above on a no-calculator section? Re-examine — a rewrite (split the fraction, trig identity, completing nothing the AP needs) is hiding.

Discrimination practice across the rational family: ∫2x/(x² - 4) dx — the numerator IS the denominator's derivative: u'/u, instant ln|x² - 4|, NO decomposition needed. ∫dx/(x² - 4) — no derivative upstairs: partial fractions over (x-2)(x+2). ∫x²/(x² - 4) — improper: divide first. Three near-identical integrands, three different routes; the discrimination is the skill, and the exam tests it explicitly.

What stays outside the AP's fence, for orientation: repeated factors (A/(x-1) + B/(x-1)²), irreducible quadratics ((Bx + C)/(x² + 1)), trig substitution, and reduction formulas — college techniques the BC exam deliberately excludes. Knowing the fence keeps preparation focused and flags any practice problem demanding more as off-syllabus.

The unit closes one chapter from here: improper integrals extend the definite integral to infinite intervals and unbounded integrands — limits meeting accumulation, with the p-series criterion that Unit 10's convergence tests will lean on. The techniques are assembled; what remains is extending where integrals are allowed to live.
key_terms: Library, substitution, u'/u, parts, rational pipeline — the AP's full kit
u'/u vs partial fractions vs divide-first: near-twins, different routes
No repeated factors, no irreducible quadratics, no trig substitution
boxes: ap_alert

Before decomposing ANY rational integrand, check the numerator against the denominator's derivative: if they match up to a constant, u-substitution finishes in one line and decomposition is wasted effort. The u'/u check costs five seconds and is the most-skipped step in the unit.

frq.question:
Consider ∫ (x³ + 2x² - x - 3)/(x(x + 1)) dx. Note the numerator has degree 3 and the denominator degree 2.
(a) Perform the polynomial division to write the integrand as a polynomial plus a proper fraction, stating your quotient and remainder.
(b) Decompose the proper remainder fraction.
(c) Assemble the complete antiderivative.
rubric: (a) (x³ + 2x² - x - 3) ÷ (x² + x) = x + 1 remainder -2x - 3: integrand = x + 1 + (-2x - 3)/(x² + x)
(c) x²/2 + x - 3 ln|x| + ln|x + 1| + C
Division verified or stated with the remainder identity
frq.model_answer: (a) Dividing x³ + 2x² - x - 3 by x² + x: first term x (giving x³ + x²), subtract: x² - x - 3; next term 1 (giving x² + x), subtract: -2x - 3. So the integrand is x + 1 + (-2x - 3)/(x(x + 1)). (b) Cover-up on (-2x - 3)/(x(x + 1)): over x, evaluate at 0: -3/1 = -3; over (x + 1), at -1: (2 - 3)/(-1) = 1. Decomposition: -3/x + 1/(x + 1). (c) ∫ = x²/2 + x - 3 ln|x| + ln|x + 1| + C.

frq.question:
A population model leads to the integral ∫ dP/(P(100 - P)) (the logistic separation, previewing Unit 7).
(a) Decompose 1/(P(100 - P)) into partial fractions. (Treat P as the variable; note the second factor is (100 - P), whose root is P = 100.)
(b) Integrate, attending to the sign produced by the (100 - P) factor.
(c) Show the antiderivative can be written as (1/100) ln|P/(100 - P)| + C.
rubric: The minus sign from d/dP(100 - P) = -1 handled explicitly
frq.model_answer: (a) Cover-up: over P, evaluate 1/(100 - P) at P = 0: 1/100. Over (100 - P), evaluate 1/P at P = 100: 1/100. So 1/(P(100 - P)) = (1/100)[1/P + 1/(100 - P)]. (b) The first piece gives (1/100)ln|P|. The second: u = 100 - P has du = -dP, so ∫dP/(100 - P) = -ln|100 - P| — sign flip from the chain rule. Total: (1/100)ln|P| - (1/100)ln|100 - P| + C. (c) Combining the logs: (1/100)ln|P/(100 - P)| + C — exactly the form Unit 7's logistic solution will exponentiate.

subject: AP Calculus BC
hook: BC ONLY: can a region stretching to infinity have finite area? Sometimes — and the difference between 1/x and 1/x² at infinity is the difference between divergence and the number 1. Improper integrals are limits wearing integral signs, and they gatekeep all of Unit 10.
learning_objectives: Define improper integrals as limits of proper integrals, with mandatory limit notation
Evaluate infinite-bound integrals and determine convergence or divergence
Handle integrands with vertical asymptotes at or inside the bounds
Apply the p-test: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges exactly when p > 1
Connect improper-integral convergence to the coming theory of infinite series

sections.title: Limits in Disguise
sections.subtitle: Defining the infinite-bound integral
sections.body:
∫₁^∞ f(x) dx is DEFINED as lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ f(x) dx: integrate to a finite cutoff b, then let the cutoff run away. If the limit exists (a finite number), the integral CONVERGES to it; if the limit is infinite or fails to exist, the integral DIVERGES. Infinity never enters an antiderivative — it enters a limit, afterward.

The headline pair: ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = lim b→∞ [-1/x]₁ᵇ = lim (1 - 1/b) = 1 — an infinite region with area exactly 1. But ∫₁^∞ dx/x = lim [ln x]₁ᵇ = lim ln b = ∞ — divergent. Both integrands die at infinity; 1/x just dies too slowly. Convergence is about the SPEED of decay, not the fact of it — the single most important intuition in the chapter and in Unit 10.

The notation is graded: writing ∫₁^∞ dx/x² = [-1/x]₁^∞ with ∞ 'plugged in' is a rubric deduction even when the answer is right. The required presentation: convert to lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ at the FIRST step, carry the b through the evaluation, take the limit LAST. Three visible stages — the AP grades the middle one specifically.

Doubly-infinite integrals split at any convenient point: ∫_{-∞}^∞ = ∫_{-∞}^0 + ∫₀^∞, each piece its own limit, and BOTH must converge for the whole to. The split discipline mirrors the piecewise splitting of chapter 4 — accumulation handles one frontier at a time.
key_terms: lim b→∞ ∫ₐᵇ f dx: a limit of proper integrals, never a plugged-in ∞
Finite limit: converges to it; infinite or nonexistent: diverges
1/x² converges, 1/x diverges — dying isn't enough; dying FAST enough is
boxes: ap_alert

The limit notation is a dedicated rubric point: 'lim b→∞' must appear BEFORE the antiderivative is evaluated, with b in the evaluation bar. The shortcut of plugging ∞ directly loses the point even with a correct final answer — every year, on every improper FRQ.

sections.title: The p-Test
sections.subtitle: The exact boundary of convergence
sections.body:
Generalizing the headline pair: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ = lim b→∞ [x^{1-p}/(1-p)]₁ᵇ for p ≠ 1. The cutoff term b^{1-p} dies when 1 - p < 0 (p > 1) and explodes when p < 1; the case p = 1 is the logarithm, divergent. The p-TEST: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges if and only if p > 1, and when it converges, its value is 1/(p - 1).

The boundary is strict and sharp: p = 1.0001 converges (to 10,000), p = 1 diverges, p = 0.9999 diverges. There is no fuzzy zone — and the same knife-edge will reappear verbatim as the p-series test in Unit 10, where Σ1/nᵖ obeys the identical criterion for the same underlying reason (the integral test will make the connection literal).

Worked contrasts cement it: ∫₁^∞ dx/x³ = 1/2 (p = 3 > 1 ✓). ∫₁^∞ dx/√x diverges (p = ½ < 1). ∫₁^∞ dx/x^{1.01} converges to 100 — barely over the line, finite all the same. Eyeballing the exponent against 1 routes the verdict in two seconds; the limit computation then certifies it for the rubric.

Exponential decay beats every power: ∫₀^∞ e^{-x} dx = lim [-e^{-x}]₀ᵇ = 1, and ∫₀^∞ e^{-kx} dx = 1/k for any k > 0. Exponentials at infinity are the friendliest integrands in the chapter — the growth hierarchy of Unit 1, now reading its decay-side consequences.
key_terms: ∫₁^∞ dx/xᵖ converges iff p > 1, to the value 1/(p - 1)
p = 1 diverges; any p > 1 converges — no fuzzy zone
∫₀^∞ e^{-kx} dx = 1/k: exponentials always converge at infinity
boxes: ap_alert

Memorize the p-test as stated — 'converges if and only if p > 1' — because Unit 10 reuses it for series verbatim, and the exam asks it in both costumes. The single criterion is worth points in two units.

sections.title: Vertical Asymptotes
sections.subtitle: When the integrand, not the bound, is infinite
sections.body:
The second improper species: a finite interval whose integrand blows up at an endpoint. ∫₀¹ dx/√x has a vertical asymptote at 0 — define it as lim a→0⁺ ∫ₐ¹ dx/√x = lim [2√x]ₐ¹ = lim (2 - 2√a) = 2. Convergent: the spike at zero is thin enough to enclose finite area. The one-sided limit approaches the singularity from inside the interval.

The endpoint p-test mirrors (and flips) the infinite-bound one: ∫₀¹ dx/xᵖ converges iff p < 1. At the singular end, SMALL p (gentle spikes) converges and large p diverges — the reverse of the behavior at infinity, because the danger zone is x near 0 where small powers are tamer. The pair of p-tests, with their opposite inequalities, is a classic discrimination question.

The hidden-singularity trap: ∫₋₁¹ dx/x² LOOKS routine, but the integrand explodes at x = 0 — inside the interval. The chapter-4 warning returns with teeth: evaluating [−1/x]₋₁¹ = -2 (negative, for a positive integrand!) is nonsense; the honest treatment splits at 0 into two improper integrals, each divergent — the integral diverges. Scanning the interval for interior singularities is mandatory before ANY evaluation bar.

Mixed cases chain the species: ∫₀^∞ dx/(√x(1 + x)) is improper at both ends, split at x = 1 into an endpoint-singular piece and an infinite-bound piece, each assessed separately. The AP keeps such doubles rare; the splitting principle is what it tests when they appear.
key_terms: lim a→r⁺ from inside: the one-sided limit version of improper
∫₀¹ dx/xᵖ converges iff p < 1 — opposite inequality at the spike
Blow-ups INSIDE the interval force a split; ignoring them yields nonsense
boxes: ap_alert

∫₋₁¹ dx/x² = -2 is the chapter's poison answer — negative area from a positive function, produced by ignoring the interior asymptote. Scan (a, b) for integrand blow-ups before every definite evaluation; the scan IS the question on several past exams.

sections.title: Convergence Without Evaluation
sections.subtitle: Comparison thinking and the bridge to series
sections.body:
Sometimes the verdict matters and the value doesn't — and comparison delivers verdicts without antiderivatives. If 0 ≤ f(x) ≤ g(x) for large x: g converging forces f to converge (trapped under a finite roof), and f diverging forces g to diverge (pushed up by an infinite floor). ∫₁^∞ dx/(x³ + 5): the integrand sits below 1/x³, whose integral converges (p = 3) — converges, no decomposition needed.

The comparison instinct: identify the integrand's DOMINANT behavior at the frontier (largest power downstairs minus upstairs, exponential factors), compare to the matching p-integral or exponential. (sin²x)/x² ≤ 1/x²: converges. (2 + cos x)/x ≥ 1/x: diverges. Bounded factors never change the verdict; the frontier behavior decides.

This is Unit 10's training ground, explicitly: series convergence runs on the same comparison logic (direct comparison, limit comparison), the same p-criterion, and the integral test literally converts series questions INTO this chapter's questions. Students solid on improper integrals find half of Unit 10 pre-learned; the investment pays forward at the course's highest-stakes unit.

The unit closes here, fully equipped: accumulation defined (ch 1), approximated (ch 2), welded to derivatives (ch 3-4), and computed by a four-technique kit (ch 5-7) that now reaches infinite domains (ch 8). Unit 7 immediately spends the equipment on differential equations — where antiderivatives become predictions and the logistic equation cashes the partial-fractions check this unit wrote.
key_terms: Under a convergent roof: converges; over a divergent floor: diverges
The integrand's behavior at ∞ (or the singularity) decides; bounded factors don't
Same logic, same p-criterion: the integral test makes the connection literal
boxes: ap_alert

'Determine whether the integral converges' does NOT always mean 'evaluate it' — comparison to a p-integral earns full credit when the question asks only for the verdict with justification. Read the ask; evaluation is sometimes the slow road to the same points.

mcq.explanation: p = 1/2 < 1: divergent by the p-test. The others: p = 1.001 > 1 ✓, exponential ✓, p = 2 ✓.

choices.A: the integrand has an asymptote at x = 0 inside the interval, so FTC2 never applied

choices.A: converges, by comparison with a convergent p-integral

frq.question:
Evaluate each improper integral or show it diverges, using complete limit notation.
(a) ∫₂^∞ dx/(x - 1)²
(b) ∫₁^∞ dx/(2x + 3)
(c) ∫₀^∞ x e^{-x²} dx
rubric: (a) lim b→∞ [-(x-1)^{-1}]₂ᵇ = 0 + 1 = 1: converges to 1
(b) lim b→∞ (1/2)[ln|2x+3|]₁ᵇ = ∞: diverges
Limit notation present at the first step in all three
frq.model_answer: (a) ∫₂^∞ dx/(x-1)² = lim b→∞ ∫₂ᵇ (x-1)^{-2} dx = lim b→∞ [-(x-1)^{-1}]₂ᵇ = lim b→∞ (1 - 1/(b-1)) = 1. Converges to 1. (b) lim b→∞ ∫₁ᵇ dx/(2x+3) = lim b→∞ (1/2)[ln(2x+3)]₁ᵇ = lim b→∞ (1/2)(ln(2b+3) - ln 5) = ∞. Diverges. (c) With u = x², du = 2x dx: lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ x e^{-x²} dx = lim b→∞ [-½e^{-x²}]₀ᵇ = lim b→∞ (½ - ½e^{-b²}) = 1/2. Converges to 1/2.

frq.question:
Consider ∫₀⁴ dx/(x - 2)^{2/3}.
(a) Explain why this integral is improper despite its finite bounds.
(b) Split appropriately and evaluate both pieces.
(c) State the value of the integral, or that it diverges.
rubric: (a) The integrand blows up at x = 2, inside [0, 4] — interior singularity
(b) Split at 2: lim t→2⁻ ∫₀ᵗ + lim s→2⁺ ∫ₛ⁴, antiderivative 3(x-2)^{1/3}
(c) Both converge: total 6·2^{1/3} = 6∛2
frq.model_answer: (a) At x = 2 — inside the interval — the denominator vanishes and the integrand is unbounded: an interior singularity makes the integral improper. (b) Split at 2. Antiderivative: ∫(x-2)^{-2/3} dx = 3(x-2)^{1/3}. Left: lim t→2⁻ [3(x-2)^{1/3}]₀ᵗ = 3(0) - 3(-2)^{1/3} = 3·2^{1/3} (since (-2)^{1/3} = -2^{1/3}). Right: lim s→2⁺ [3(x-2)^{1/3}]ₛ⁴ = 3·2^{1/3} - 0 = 3·2^{1/3}. (c) Both one-sided pieces converge, so the integral converges: 3·2^{1/3} + 3·2^{1/3} = 6∛2 ≈ 7.56. (The exponent 2/3 < 1 at the spike is why convergence was possible.)

frq.question:
A pollutant enters a lake at rate R(t) = 40/(t + 1)² grams per day, for t ≥ 0.
(a) Find the total amount of pollutant that will EVER enter the lake — set up and evaluate the appropriate improper integral.
(b) Find the time T by which half of that total has entered.
(c) The cleanup agency claims 'the inflow never stops, so the total grows without bound.' Refute the claim in one sentence using the chapter's central distinction.
rubric: (a) lim b→∞ ∫₀ᵇ 40(t+1)^{-2} dt = lim [−40/(t+1)]₀ᵇ = 40 grams
(c) A perpetual inflow with sufficiently fast decay accumulates a finite total
The decay-speed (not decay-fact) distinction articulated
frq.model_answer: (a) Total = ∫₀^∞ 40/(t+1)² dt = lim b→∞ [−40/(t+1)]₀ᵇ = lim b→∞ (40 - 40/(b+1)) = 40 grams. (b) Accumulated by time T: 40 - 40/(T+1). Setting it to 20: 40/(T+1) = 20, T + 1 = 2, T = 1 day — half of all the pollutant that will ever arrive comes in the first day. (c) The claim confuses 'never stops' with 'adds up to infinity': the inflow rate decays fast enough (like 1/t², p = 2 > 1) that the endless trickle accumulates only a finite 40 grams — convergence is about decay speed, not stopping.
